name: Tibolone (Livial)
lead: Tibolone, sold as Livial and under other brand names, is an oral synthetic steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity, classed as a selective tissue estrogenic activity regulator (STEAR). It is prescribed to postmenopausal women for hot flushes, vaginal atrophy and prevention of osteoporosis [1][2].

It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in the Netherlands in 1988 and the UK in 1991. It is not approved in the United States, is a Canadian Schedule IV controlled substance because it is classed as an anabolic steroid, and is prohibited by WADA [1][2].

Large randomised trials and observational studies have examined its benefits and risks in menopausal women.[3][4][5] Its relevance to looks is through hormonal status: by relieving menopausal symptoms and protecting bone, it is part of how some postmenopausal women manage the changes that come with oestrogen loss, and its mild androgenic activity and anabolic-steroid classification explain why it is mentioned in muscle-related contexts. No studies were found of tibolone for appearance or physique in men or women.

paras: Tibolone is indicated for menopausal vasomotor and urogenital symptoms and for prevention of osteoporosis in women at risk of fractures who cannot use other therapies [1][2]. It has also been studied for sexual function and mood in postmenopausal women [1][2].

Tibolone itself is inactive; it is converted to 3-alpha- and 3-beta-hydroxytibolone (estrogenic) and the delta-4 isomer (progestogenic and androgenic). Tissue-selective activity gives effects on bone, brain and vagina with less stimulation of the uterus and breast [1][6]. Wikipedia reports a half-life of about 45 hours and a roughly 50 percent reduction in SHBG [1].

Because the parent drug is inactive and its three metabolites differ in receptor activity, tibolone is described as tissue-selective; the 2001 review in the Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology frames this as a steroid with a tissue-specific mode of action.[6]

sections.h: Effects on skin, hair, libido and mood
paras: Because tibolone has weak androgenic activity, Wikipedia reports acne and increased facial hair infrequently, in about 3 to 6 percent of treated women.[1] It also reports positive effects on mood and sexual function, with libido possibly improving more than on standard menopausal hormone therapy, a difference attributed to the androgenic metabolites; tibolone has been investigated as a possible treatment for female sexual dysfunction.[1] Changes in blood markers listed on the page include roughly a 30 percent fall in HDL cholesterol, a 20 percent fall in triglycerides and about a 50 percent fall in sex hormone-binding globulin.[1]

Tibolone is a synthetic estrane steroid derived from 19-nortestosterone, specifically the 7-alpha-methyl derivative of noretynodrel, with the formula C21H28O2 and a molar mass of about 312 g/mol; related steroids include trestolone and mibolerone.[1]

Wikipedia reports oral bioavailability of about 92 percent, 96 percent plasma protein binding mostly to albumin, conversion in liver and intestine to 3-alpha-hydroxytibolone, 3-beta-hydroxytibolone and delta-4-tibolone, peak levels one to two hours after a single oral tablet, and an elimination half-life of about 45 hours, with excretion roughly 40 percent in urine and 60 percent in faeces.[1]

Androgenic effects such as acne and facial hair occur in a minority of women, and unscheduled bleeding is common [1]. A 2016 Cochrane review linked tibolone to higher rates of stroke, cardiovascular events and endometrial cancer, though much of the evidence was low quality; breast cancer findings have been mixed [1]. Contraindications include breast cancer, thromboembolic disease and undiagnosed vaginal bleeding [2].

Wikipedia gives odds ratios from the 2016 Cochrane review of 1.74 for stroke, 1.38 for cardiovascular events, 2.04 for endometrial cancer and 1.5 for breast cancer in women with a prior history (0.52 in women without), noting most rest on very low-quality evidence; unscheduled vaginal bleeding is common, with an odds ratio of 2.79.[1]

The LIFT trial randomised 4,538 women aged 60 to 85 with osteoporosis (a hip or spine T score of -2.5 or lower, or -2.0 or lower with radiologic evidence of vertebral fracture) to tibolone or placebo and examined fractures, breast cancer and cardiovascular events;[3] it was reported to show fewer vertebral fractures and breast cancers alongside an increased stroke risk. The LIBERATE trial (n = 3,148) in women with a history of breast cancer examined recurrence and symptom relief and reported a higher recurrence rate with tibolone.[4][7]

The Million Women Study observational data included tibolone in analyses of breast cancer (1,084,110 UK women aged 50 to 64) and of endometrial cancer (716,738 postmenopausal women without hysterectomy).[5][8] An eight-year clinical experience report reviewed 301 postmenopausal women treated with tibolone, most of whom had not previously received climacteric therapy.[11]

Smaller studies have looked at endometrial effects,[12] mammographic breast density,[13] homocysteine levels,[14] HDL cholesterol (n=20),[18] vascular function (n=60),[19] bone density versus raloxifene (n=324),[9] bone density, symptoms and breast density after prophylactic oophorectomy (n=50),[17] the endometrium (n=32),[20] and menopausal depression (n=120).[10] Reviews cover tibolone in osteoporosis and in breast cancer.[15][16] No studies were found of tibolone for appearance or muscle.

Tibolone was developed in the 1960s at Organon, whose 1967 patent covers the original synthesis, under the development code Org OD14; it was introduced in the Netherlands in 1988 and the UK in 1991 and is now marketed across the EU, Asia and Australasia.[1] Wikipedia lists it for menopausal symptoms, postmenopausal osteoporosis and endometriosis.[1]

Tibolone's classification as an anabolic steroid in Canada and its WADA prohibition are the main links to athletic contexts [1]. The FDA did not authorise it in the US after 2006 on safety grounds, according to Grokipedia [2].

Brand names include Livial, Tibofem, Tibella and Ladybon.[1] It is listed in the infobox as prescription-only in the UK and Australia, a Schedule IV controlled substance in Canada, and not available in the US.[1]

Wikipedia describes the Canadian Schedule IV listing under the 1996 Controlled Drugs and Substances Act as an anabolic steroid, noting it is the only norethisterone derivative so classified, and attributes the WADA ban in category S1 largely to its conversion to an androgenic metabolite.[1] In Australia it is Schedule 4 with pregnancy category D, and in the UK it is a prescription-only medicine.[1]

card.summary: A menopause drug with weak androgenic activity; heavily trialled for menopause, never for looks.
card.note: Not approved in the US; trials link it to stroke and breast cancer recurrence in specific groups.

quick.overview:
Tibolone is a prescription hormone therapy for menopause symptoms and osteoporosis in many countries, though not the US.

It has weak androgenic activity and is classed as an anabolic steroid in Canada, but no studies test it for appearance or muscle.
quick.mechanism: It is a prodrug whose metabolites act on estrogen, progesterone and androgen receptors in tissue-selective ways, and it lowers SHBG.
quick.risks: Trials and reviews report increased stroke risk in older women, higher breast cancer recurrence in survivors, and endometrial cancer and bleeding concerns. Acne and facial hair occur in some women.

chain: Tibolone metabolites act on oestrogen, progesterone and androgen receptors
Hot flushes, vaginal atrophy and bone loss are reduced
Postmenopausal women maintain comfort and bone health
angle.text: Tibolone is prescribed to postmenopausal women to relieve hormonal symptoms and protect bone. Its androgenic component is the reason it is sometimes mentioned in muscle-related discussions; this is a description of how it is talked about, not a demonstrated cosmetic use.
